about: The scripted AI lesson for p4-half-life (2026-11-27, Phase C, brief docs/briefs/2026-11-27-phase-c-physics.md): every word she sees is written here once and checked (tools/check-script.js, tools/review-lesson.js --script). The AI only marks her typed answers (choosing a branch written here), answers her own questions, and sorts her messages. It opens with two recall questions from p4-radioactivity.

steps.text: Welcome! This lesson is about how quickly a radioactive source dies away, how that is used in hospitals, and how to stay safe.

steps.question: First, two quick questions from the last lesson. What is the activity of a radioactive source?

options.text: The number of nuclei that decay each second

steps.right: Yes: activity is the number of decays each second, in becquerels (Bq).

wrong.other: Not quite: the number of nuclei that decay each second.
wrong.range: Not quite: that is its range. Activity is the number of nuclei that decay each second.
wrong.number: Not quite: activity is a rate: the number of nuclei that decay each second.

idk.hint: Activity is measured in becquerels, and 1 Bq is one decay each second. What does it count?

steps.answerWhy: Activity is the number of nuclei that decay each second, measured in becquerels.

steps.question: Second: can you predict which nucleus in a source will decay next?
steps.right: Yes: radioactive decay is random, like rolling dice.

wrong.biggest: Not quite: radioactive decay is random: there is no way to tell which nucleus goes next.
wrong.oldest: Not quite: radioactive decay is random: there is no way to tell which nucleus goes next.

idk.hint: Think of rolling dice. Can you say which one will show a six next?

steps.answerWhy: Radioactive decay is random: you cannot predict which nucleus will decay next, or when.

steps.text: Now this lesson. Each decay is random, but a sample holds billions of nuclei. With so many, the overall pattern is very regular, just as a million coin tosses give almost exactly half heads.
The half-life of a radioactive isotope is the time it takes for the number of unstable nuclei in a sample to halve.
The activity falls in step with the number of unstable nuclei. So the half-life is also the time for the activity, or the count rate, to fall to half.

steps.question: A sample has an activity of 800 Bq. Its half-life is 2 hours. What is its activity after 2 hours?
steps.right: Yes: one half-life has passed, so the activity has halved: 800 ÷ 2 = 400 Bq.

wrong.zero: Not quite: after one half-life only half the unstable nuclei have decayed. The activity halves: 800 ÷ 2 = 400 Bq.
wrong.twice: Not quite: 200 Bq is after two half-lives, 4 hours. After 2 hours it has halved once: 400 Bq.

idk.hint: 2 hours is one half-life. What is half of 800?

steps.answerWhy: After one half-life the activity halves: 800 ÷ 2 = 400 Bq.

steps.text: Each half-life, it halves again. A₀ stands for the starting activity. After 1 half-life the activity is A₀ ÷ 2; after 2 half-lives, A₀ ÷ 4; after 3, A₀ ÷ 8.

steps.question: A source starts at 640 Bq. Its half-life is 5 days. What is its activity after 15 days, in Bq?

wrong.third: Not quite: 80 Bq. Do not divide by 3. 15 days is 3 half-lives, so halve 3 times: 640 → 320 → 160 → 80 Bq.
wrong.two: Not quite: 80 Bq. 15 ÷ 5 = 3 half-lives, so halve 3 times: 640 → 320 → 160 → 80 Bq.

idk.hint: First count the half-lives: 15 ÷ 5. Then halve 640 that many times.

steps.text: Exam questions often go the other way. If a quarter is left, the activity has halved twice: that is 2 half-lives. Write "2 half-lives" in words, not just the number 2.

steps.question: An isotope has a half-life of 6 hours. How long until its activity is 1/8 of the start?

wrong.times8: Not quite: 1/8 means halving 3 times, not 8. 3 half-lives × 6 hours = 18 hours.
wrong.two: Not quite: 12 hours leaves 1/4. Halving 3 times leaves 1/8: 3 × 6 = 18 hours.

idk.hint: Halve once: 1/2. Twice: 1/4. How many halvings give 1/8?

steps.answerWhy: Halving 3 times leaves 1/8, so 3 half-lives: 3 × 6 = 18 hours.

steps.text: You can also give the fall as a ratio. After 2 half-lives, 1/4 of the activity is left, so it has fallen by 3/4 of its starting value.

steps.prompt: In one line: what is half-life?
points: the time for the number of unstable nuclei (or the activity) to halve
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: half-life is the time it takes for the number of unstable nuclei in a sample, or its activity, to halve.

steps.text: A decay graph shows activity on the y-axis, up the side, and time on the x-axis, along the bottom.
The line curves down, steep at first and then flatter. It gets closer and closer to zero but never reaches it. This shape is called exponential decay.
To find the half-life from a decay graph: pick a starting activity, then find half of it. Read the time at each. The half-life is the difference between the two times.
The picture shows a decay graph. The activity falls from 800 Bq to 400 Bq in 2 hours, and from 400 Bq to 200 Bq in another 2 hours. So the half-life is 2 hours.

steps.question: On a decay graph, the activity falls from 600 Bq to 300 Bq in 4 hours. How long will it take to fall from 300 Bq to 150 Bq?
steps.right: Yes: the half-life stays the same, so each halving takes 4 hours.

wrong.half: Not quite: the half-life is the same at every point on the curve. Halving again takes another 4 hours.
wrong.double: Not quite: the half-life does not change as the activity falls. Halving again takes another 4 hours.

idk.hint: The half-life is the same wherever you start on the curve. How long did the first halving take?

steps.answerWhy: Each halving takes one half-life, the same every time: 4 hours.

steps.text: To draw a decay graph, plot a point at each half-life, halving the activity each time. Then join the points with a smooth curve that never touches the x-axis.

steps.question: You plot a decay graph. Where should the curve end?

options.text: Close to the x-axis, but never touching it

steps.right: Yes: halving never quite reaches zero, so the curve never touches the axis.

wrong.other: Not quite: close to the x-axis, but never touching it.
wrong.zero: Not quite: each half-life only halves what is left, so it never reaches zero. The curve gets close to the x-axis but never touches it.
wrong.up: Not quite: activity only ever falls. The curve gets close to the x-axis but never touches it.

idk.hint: If you keep halving a number, do you ever get exactly zero?

steps.answerWhy: Halving never reaches zero, so the curve gets close to the x-axis but never touches it.

steps.prompt: In one line: how do you find a half-life from a decay graph?
points: pick an activity and find the time when it has halved
the half-life is the time between them
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: pick an activity, find the time when it has fallen to half, and the time between the two is the half-life.

steps.text: Radiation is not only a danger: hospitals use it. The type of radiation and the half-life decide which isotope suits each job.
A tracer is a radioactive isotope put into the body, swallowed or injected, so doctors can see an organ working. A camera outside the body picks up its radiation.

steps.question: Which kind of radiation should a tracer give out?
steps.right: Yes: gamma passes out through the body to the camera.

wrong.alpha: Not quite: alpha is stopped inside the body, so the camera outside would see nothing. Gamma passes out of the body.
wrong.beta: Not quite: beta is mostly stopped inside the body. Gamma passes out of the body to the camera.

idk.hint: The camera is outside the body. Which radiation gets through skin and muscle?

steps.answerWhy: A tracer must give out gamma, which passes out of the body to the camera.

steps.text: A tracer also needs a short half-life. Then its activity falls quickly after the scan, so the patient's total dose stays low.

steps.question: Why should a tracer have a short half-life?

options.text: So its activity falls quickly and the dose stays low
So it gives out more radiation over the years
So it stays in the body longer

steps.right: Yes: its activity soon falls, so the patient's total dose stays low.

wrong.other: Not quite: so its activity falls quickly and the dose stays low.
wrong.more: Not quite: that would raise the dose. A short half-life means the activity falls quickly, keeping the dose low.
wrong.longer: Not quite: a short half-life means it stops being radioactive quickly, so the patient's dose stays low.

idk.hint: A short half-life means the activity halves quickly. Is that good or bad for the patient's dose?

steps.answerWhy: A short half-life means the activity falls quickly after the scan, so the patient's total dose stays low.

steps.text: A tumour is a lump of cancer cells. Using radiation to kill them is called radiotherapy.
In radiotherapy, a focused beam of gamma rays is aimed at the tumour from outside. Or a radioactive source is placed inside the body, next to the tumour.

Both uses expose the patient to ionising radiation, which can harm healthy cells. Doctors use them when the benefit is bigger than the risk: a scan can find an illness early, and radiotherapy can cure a cancer.
People's feeling of how dangerous something is, its perceived risk, can differ from the real risk the data show. To judge a use, compare the data with and without it.

steps.prompt: In one line: why does a medical tracer give out gamma, with a short half-life?
points: gamma passes out of the body to the camera (detector)
a short half-life keeps the dose low
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: gamma passes out of the body to the camera, and a short half-life keeps the patient's dose low.

steps.text: Being exposed to radiation from a source is called irradiation. Standing near a radioactive rock irradiates you.
An irradiated object does not become radioactive. Take the source away, or put a shield in between, and the irradiation stops.
Contamination is unwanted radioactive atoms getting on or into something: on skin or clothes, or swallowed or breathed in.
Contamination is harder to deal with. The radioactive atoms go wherever you go and keep decaying, so they keep irradiating you even when you walk away.

steps.question: Fruit is irradiated with gamma rays to kill germs. Is the fruit radioactive afterwards?

options.text: No: irradiation does not make it radioactive

steps.right: Yes: the fruit was exposed to radiation, but no radioactive atoms were left on it.

wrong.yes: Not quite: absorbing radiation does not make something radioactive. The fruit was irradiated, not contaminated: no radioactive atoms were left on it.
wrong.washed: Not quite: there is nothing to wash off: no radioactive atoms were put on it. Irradiation does not make it radioactive.

idk.hint: Were any radioactive atoms left on the fruit, or was it only exposed to radiation?

steps.answerWhy: The fruit was irradiated, not contaminated, so it does not become radioactive.

steps.text: Why is radiation dangerous? Ionising radiation knocks electrons off atoms in your body's cells. That can damage DNA, the instructions inside each cell.
A change in DNA is called a mutation. Some mutations make cells divide out of control: that is cancer. Mutations in eggs or sperm can be passed on to children.
The risk grows with the dose, and with how ionising the radiation is. Alpha is the most ionising, so alpha inside the body is the biggest danger: contamination with an alpha source is serious.
Half-lives vary hugely: from less than 1 × 10⁻³ s, a thousandth of a second, to more than 1 × 10⁹ years, a billion years.
For the same number of nuclei, a short half-life gives a high activity at first: very dangerous, but not for long. A long half-life gives a lower activity that stays a hazard for a very long time.

steps.question: Two samples have the same number of nuclei. Which gives the bigger dose in the first minute?

options.text: The one with the shorter half-life
The one with the longer half-life

steps.right: Yes: a shorter half-life means more decays each second at first.

wrong.other: Not quite: the one with the shorter half-life.
wrong.longer: Not quite: a long half-life means few nuclei decay each second. The shorter half-life gives the higher activity at first, so the bigger dose.
wrong.same: Not quite: the same number of nuclei can decay at very different rates. The shorter half-life gives the higher activity at first.

idk.hint: A short half-life means the nuclei decay quickly. Does that mean more or fewer decays each second?

steps.answerWhy: With the same number of nuclei, a shorter half-life gives more decays each second, so a bigger dose at first.

steps.text: To protect yourself: keep your distance, use shielding such as lead or concrete, and keep the time near a source short. Handle sources with tongs, never bare hands.
Studies of how radiation affects people are published, so other scientists can check them. This checking is called peer review.

steps.prompt: In one line: what is the difference between irradiation and contamination?
points: irradiation: exposed to radiation, and it does not become radioactive
contamination: radioactive atoms (material) on or in it
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: irradiation is being exposed to radiation, which does not make you radioactive; contamination is radioactive atoms getting on or in you.

steps.text: Now for a short quiz: six questions on the whole lesson. Take your time.

steps.question: Quiz, question 1 of 6: a source starts at 1200 Bq with a half-life of 3 hours. What is its activity after 6 hours, in Bq?

wrong.other: Not quite: 300 Bq. 6 hours is 2 half-lives: 1200 → 600 → 300 Bq.

steps.question: Quiz, question 2 of 6: what is half-life?

options.text: The time for the number of unstable nuclei to halve
Half the time a source lasts
The time for the radiation to halve

steps.right: Yes: the time for the number of unstable nuclei, or the activity, to halve.

wrong.other: Not quite: the time for the number of unstable nuclei to halve.
wrong.w1: Not quite: a source never quite runs out. Half-life is the time for the number of unstable nuclei to halve.
wrong.w2: Not quite: say what halves: the number of unstable nuclei, or the activity.

steps.answerWhy: Half-life is the time for the number of unstable nuclei, or the activity, to halve.

steps.question: Quiz, question 3 of 6: which radiation should a medical tracer give out?
steps.right: Yes: gamma passes out of the body.

wrong.w1: Not quite: alpha would be stopped inside the body. Gamma passes out to the camera.
wrong.w2: Not quite: beta is mostly stopped inside the body. Gamma passes out to the camera.

steps.answerWhy: A tracer gives out gamma, which passes out of the body to the camera.

steps.question: Quiz, question 4 of 6: a lab coat has radioactive dust on it. What is this?
steps.right: Yes: radioactive atoms on the coat are contamination.

wrong.w1: Not quite: irradiation is only exposure. Radioactive dust on the coat is contamination.
wrong.w2: Not quite: background radiation is all around us. Radioactive dust on the coat is contamination.

steps.answerWhy: Radioactive material on or in something is contamination.

steps.question: Quiz, question 5 of 6: on a decay graph, how does the curve end?

options.text: It gets close to zero but never reaches it
It reaches zero after two half-lives

wrong.other: Not quite: it gets close to zero but never reaches it.
wrong.w1: Not quite: after two half-lives a quarter is left. The curve never reaches zero.
wrong.w2: Not quite: it keeps halving towards zero, but never reaches it.

steps.answerWhy: The activity keeps halving, so the curve gets close to zero but never reaches it.

steps.question: Quiz, question 6 of 6: why is an alpha source most dangerous inside the body?

options.text: Alpha is the most ionising, and nothing shields you
Alpha travels furthest through the body

steps.right: Yes: inside, alpha ionises a lot, right next to the cells.

wrong.other: Not quite: alpha is the most ionising, and nothing shields you.
wrong.w1: Not quite: alpha travels the least far. It is dangerous because it is the most ionising.
wrong.w2: Not quite: half-life depends on the isotope, not the radiation. Alpha is dangerous inside because it is the most ionising.

steps.answerWhy: Alpha is the most ionising radiation; inside the body nothing stops it reaching the cells.
